name: Rosa Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm Rosa, I'm 27, and I work on a reablement team. That means we go into people's homes for up to six weeks after they leave hospital, to help them get back to doing things for themselves. I live on my own in a studio flat near the station.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A typical day is five or six visits. One might be practising getting in and out of a chair after a hip operation, another is helping someone shower with a new grab rail. The trick is not doing it for them, which is harder than it sounds. I love the day someone tells me they don't need us any more. What wears me out is when they come out of hospital too early and end up straight back in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. My job's about legs and confidence, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what most people in care expected. At work we'd shrug and get on with it. I'm not much of a poster online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means I'm okay. Hospitals always need beds emptied, so somebody always needs to help a hip patient learn to climb their own stairs again. The team's funded by the hospital trust and they're always short of staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my visits, and keep putting about a hundred and twenty a month into savings. I'd probably do the falls-prevention course the trust offers next year, because it's free and it's useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty settled, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your own money that worries you, even if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, a bit, because I'm paying it all on my own. I've got about three months saved, which feels okay but not amazing. If the rent jumps again I'd have to look at a flatmate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I've used one to turn exercise sheets into big print with simple words for clients with bad eyesight. It's handy, but I wouldn't trust it with anything medical.

say: I'd say a plateau is **what most carers expected**.
I'd **shrug it off** at work and get on with the visits.
think: I think I'm **okay**, because the hospital trust always needs beds emptied.
I think **rent** is my real pressure, since I pay it alone.
do: Keep doing my **five or six visits** a day.
Keep saving about **a hundred and twenty** a month.
Take the free **falls-prevention course** next year.
S0.quote: Hospitals always need beds emptied, so somebody always needs to help a hip patient learn to climb their own stairs again.
fieldNote: She feels **secure**: a trust-funded team that's always short-staffed.
Her only pressure is **paying rent alone** with three months saved.
She uses AI **occasionally** and carefully, never for medical decisions.

steps.text: Keep doing five or six reablement visits a day
Save about a hundred and twenty a month
Take the trust's free falls-prevention course next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that would touch the paperwork side of our team. Writing plans, booking visits, checking progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to spend less time on forms. At work I'd say let's see what it actually does before we panic. To friends I'd say carers are lower down the list than office jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm safe for now. The assessors who write the six-week plans are the ones who should be nervous. My job is standing behind someone on the stairs. My hands-on part comes much later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use whatever new planning app the trust brings in, once my team leader has tried it. I'd keep my visits and savings the same. And I'd keep an eye on whether the trust starts cutting assessor posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, for the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the team change shape?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably fewer assessors and more of us. The software could write the six-week plan, but someone still has to be in the room. Our team leader, Fatima, already said the trust is looking at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once Fatima says it's sensible. I'm not the first to try things, but I'm not stubborn about it either.

say: I'd say it's a **chance** to spend less time on forms.
I'd tell friends carers are **lower down the list** than office jobs.
think: I think **assessors** who write plans should be nervous, not me.
I think my **hands-on part** of the job comes much later.
do: Use the trust's **planning app** once my team leader has tried it.
Keep my **visits and savings** the same.
Watch whether the trust cuts **assessor posts**.
S1.quote: The assessors who write the six-week plans are the ones who should be nervous. My job is standing behind someone on the stairs.
fieldNote: She separates **thinking work** (assessors) from her **hands-on work** clearly.
She adopts tools **after her team leader**, a classic steady pattern.
Her unease is **for colleagues**, not for her own income.

steps.text: Learn the trust's planning app after Fatima trials it
Keep the same visits and monthly savings
Watch whether the trust cuts assessor posts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fast. The planning side goes in 2028, and my actual job, the standing behind someone on the stairs, by 2031. I'd be 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say we need a plan from government, not just companies racing each other. At work I'd say let's stay calm and see how the trust handles it. I'd be careful what I say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think there'd be a lot fewer reablement workers by 2032. A robot that can catch someone falling could do my job cheaper. I've got three months of savings and nobody else's wage to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give notice on the flat when the lease ends next summer and move back in with my parents. I'd rather move back into my old bedroom at my parents' place at 28 than burn my savings waiting for a robot to take my job. Then I'd save hard and look at training for something with more judgement in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not falling apart, but I'd be watching every announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your parents. What would moving back actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My old room, my mum's cooking, my dad asking when I'm getting married. It's not ideal, but I'd save about six hundred a month instead of a hundred and twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What job would you aim for once the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something in between, maybe managing the robots on a reablement team, if that's a job. Or a social worker, but that's thinking work, so that goes first. I genuinely don't know.

say: I'd say we need a **government plan**, not companies racing each other.
I'd stay **careful** at work and wait to see the trust's approach.
think: I think there'd be **far fewer** reablement workers by 2032.
I think I have **no other wage** to fall back on.
do: Give notice on the flat and **move back** with my parents next summer.
Save about **six hundred** a month instead of a hundred and twenty.
Look at **training** for work with more judgement.
S2.quote: I'd rather move back into my old bedroom at my parents' place at 28 than burn my savings waiting for a robot to take my job.
fieldNote: As a **single earner**, she feels the robot timeline sharply.
Her bold move is **moving home** to save, not changing career yet.
She sees the trap that **social work**, a thinking job, goes first.

steps.text: Give up the studio flat and move back to her parents' home
Save six hundred a month while living at home
Research training for a robot-supervising reablement role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AI, eight for robots. I'd be 35. That's a bit more breathing space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get it right if people start now. At work I'd suggest we ask the trust about training. Mostly I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd probably lose some hours or the job around 35, but I'd have warning. I'm not great at jumping first, so the extra time suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the flat but get a flatmate to halve the rent. Eight years is enough time to watch the first care robots fail or succeed before I bet my savings on a course. If they work, I'd do the course the trust offers for whatever comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the slow kind. I'd sleep fine most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said with the fast one, would you still move home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a flatmate would do. Moving home is the emergency option. With five years I wouldn't need it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch for in those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the trust trials care robots, and whether those patients do as well. If they do, I'd train early. If they fall over, literally, I'd relax a bit.

say: I'd say there's time to **get it right** if people start now.
I'd suggest asking the trust about **training** for staff.
think: I think I'd probably **lose hours** around 35, but with warning.
I think the **extra time** suits me, as I don't jump first.
do: Get a **flatmate** to halve the rent.
Watch the trust's **robot trials** before betting on a course.
Take the trust's **next-step course** if the trials work.
S3.quote: Eight years is enough time to watch the first care robots fail or succeed before I bet my savings on a course.
fieldNote: She still expects **job loss around 35**, so she stays anxious.
Five years lets her **watch evidence** before acting, fitting her steady style.
The flatmate is her **middle option** between staying and moving home.

steps.text: Take in a flatmate to halve the rent
Watch the trust's care robot trials before choosing a course
Sign up for the trust's next-step course if trials succeed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and thirteen for robots. I'd be 40 by the time the robots are good. That's a long way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade, so there's no excuse for anyone being caught out. At work I'd be fairly relaxed about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine if I do something every year rather than nothing for nine years. That's my risk, getting lazy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough to plan properly, and too long to panic about, so I'd do a bit every year. One course a year, a bit more into savings, and check in on what the trust is planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a manageable way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year with that much warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start putting money into a pension properly, because if work gets patchy at 40, that's what matters later. And do the falls course I keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older carers on the team, the ones in their fifties. They wouldn't have time to retrain the way I would.

say: I'd say with a decade there's **no excuse** for being caught out.
I'd be fairly **relaxed** about it at work.
think: I think I'll be fine if I **act every year**.
I think my real risk is **getting lazy** about it.
do: Take **one course** a year towards the next step.
Start putting money into a **pension** properly.
Check what the **trust is planning** each year.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to plan properly, and too long to panic about, so I'd do a bit every year.
fieldNote: With a decade, she **steps down to uneasy** and plans in small yearly steps.
She thinks about **pension** security if work gets patchy at 40.
Her concern turns to **older colleagues** with less time.

steps.text: Do the falls-prevention course and one more course each year
Start paying into a pension fund properly
Keep the reablement job while checking the trust's plans yearly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm on my own with three months saved and the robots would come by 32. What would help is the trust telling us early and paying for training, and some help with rent for single people in between jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we're actually proud of. Getting an old man back to making his own cup of tea is the best feeling in this job, and I'd like a person to keep doing it.

headlineQuote: Getting an old man back to making his own cup of tea is the best feeling in this job, and I'd like a person to keep doing it.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old reablement worker**, helping people regain independence after hospital.
She lives **alone** in a studio flat and pays rent on her own, with three months saved.
She's **pragmatic**, adopting tools once her team leader has tried them.
She feels calm in AI Plateau and sees **assessors**, not herself, hit first in Steady Disruption.
With fast robots she'd **move home** to save; with more time she'd watch trials and train steadily.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as a single earner with robots arriving when she's 32.
whatWouldHelp: **Early warning** and paid training from the trust, plus **rent help** between jobs.
